newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's debt-cutting plan puzzles analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's debt-cutting plan puzzles analysts.

text.p: A plan announced this week by Brazilian policy-makers to issue fresh foreign debt to pay down expensive domestic debt has puzzled analysts who say the scheme runs counter to the country's ongoing inflation fight.
"From an economic standpoint this doesn't make any sense," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief JP Morgan economist in Brazil.

The problem, economists say, is that bringing in dollars to retire local debt would expand the money supply unless the government issued even more domestic bonds to "sterilize" the dollar inflows, which would defeat the purpose of the plan.
"It sounds odd to me," said Manoel Alvaro, head of research at Chase Manhattan Bank in Brazil.
In principle, the idea of reducing expensive short-term domestic debt with cheap long-term foreign debt is sound and many Brazilian companies have done so over the past year.
But analysts said Brazil as a nation had not advanced far enough on the inflation front to permit the government to adopt the same policy.
"The question is are the monetary conditions ready to increase the money supply by bringing dollars in? In the long term it might be possible, but not soon," Chase's Alvaro said.

Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola said Sunday during an International Monetary Fund conference in Washington that Brazil was close to issuing $750 million of 5-to 10-year bonds in the U.S. market.
Proceeds from the so-called yankee bonds would be used to retire part of Brazil's mammoth 210 billion reais ($205 billion) domestic debt, Loyola said.

Brazil's internal debt has grown dramatically over the past 16 months largely because the Central Bank has had to issue domestic debt to soak up heavy dollar inflows, attracted by high interest rates, and prevent them from expanding the money supply.

In September, Brazil's monetary base contracted, dollar inflows slowed and monthly inflation rates fell to below 1.0 percent from 50 percent. But economists said the Central Bank was still not in a position to let the money supply expand substantially.

They speculated that the Central Bank may use a fraction of the yankee bond proceeds to pay down local debt, but that the bulk of the $750 million raised would go toward paying off interest payments on dollar-denominated Brady bonds this month.
"Their intentions aren't quite clear, but it is more likely they will use the funds to make interest payments on Brady bonds," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist at MCM Consultores in Brazil.
Rappaport said Brazil owes some $1.2 billion in Brady interest payments on Oct 15.
Some economists, however, said that if the government were to retire domestic debt with fresh foreign debt, there would be no better time to do so than now.

"If you asked me three months ago I would say no, but today it makes sense with reserves not growing anymore and the monetary base contracting," said an economist at a leading Brazilian bank who asked not to be named.
